opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's a really illustrative case, because the political incentives were enormously aligned with speed. Trump very much wanted vaccines out before the 2020 election, and Operation Warp Speed was actually one of the more successful parts of the response: funding manufacturing at risk, in parallel with the trials, so doses were ready the moment approval came. But there was still a lot of value left on the table, and I think much of that was a failure of information and advice rather than of motivation.

Imagine he'd had access to AI advisors that were trustworthy, that he could query at length, and that could explain things to him in terms of his own interests. They could have said: "Look, Mr. President, the Moderna vaccine was designed in a couple of days in January 2020. The bottleneck isn't the science, it's the testing and regulatory process and manufacturing capacity. Here are the options." One option would have been human challenge trials, deliberately exposing consenting young volunteers, which could have compressed months of efficacy testing into weeks. Another would have been scaling manufacturing far more aggressively and earlier, buying capacity for many candidates at once, because the cost of a few tens of billions of dollars was trivial next to the trillions in economic damage and the enormous loss of life. Others were things like approving on the basis of interim data sooner, or fractional dosing and first-doses-first strategies to stretch supply.

The key point is that an advisor could have laid out the expected value calculation clearly: each month of delay costs on the order of so many lives and so many hundreds of billions of dollars, and the risks of moving faster are modest by comparison. And crucially, it could have shown him that this served his goals. If vaccines had arrived in, say, summer 2020, the election might well have gone differently. So you didn't need to change his values at all. You just needed to give him accurate, accessible information about how to get what he already wanted.

That points to something more general I find hopeful about AI advice. A lot of bad policy comes not from leaders having terrible goals but from them being poorly informed, surrounded by advisors with their own institutional incentives, like regulators who get blamed for approving something harmful but not for the invisible deaths from delay. An AI advisor that's genuinely honest and that the decision-maker trusts could cut through a lot of that, and help even quite self-interested actors find the options that are good for them and good for the world at the same time.

Of course, that depends on the AIs actually being trustworthy and on people being able to verify that, which is a big part of why I think investing in honest, well-calibrated AI systems is so important.

r001.rationale: It connects Trump’s desire for vaccines before the election with AI advice tailored to his interests, and says earlier vaccine availability could have changed the election.

r002.rationale: It says human challenge trials could compress months of efficacy testing into weeks, supporting earlier vaccine deployment.

r003.rationale: It identifies testing, regulation, and manufacturing as bottlenecks and names specific options, including challenge trials, earlier interim-data approval, and expanded manufacturing.

fable-5.1.text:
So one thing worth saying up front is that, by the standards of what governments usually manage, Operation Warp Speed was actually a success. The vaccines arrived in under a year, which almost nobody in the public health establishment thought was realistic in early 2020. But it's also true that it was a success relative to a very low bar, and there were enormous amounts of value left on the table.

Think about what the actual bottlenecks were. The mRNA vaccine candidates were designed within days of the sequence being published in January. Moderna had its candidate essentially ready by mid-January. And then we spent the rest of the year on trials, on manufacturing scale-up, and on regulatory process, while something like a million-plus people were dying globally every few months and the world economy was losing trillions of dollars.

So where would AI advisors have changed things? A few places.

First, on the economics. There was a group of economists, people like Michael Kremer and Alex Tabarrok and others, who were arguing very loudly that the government should be spending vastly more on manufacturing capacity in advance, before we knew which vaccines worked. The logic is straightforward: if the pandemic is costing you trillions, and the entire budget for buying out all the world's vaccine production capacity is in the tens of billions, you should be building factories for every plausible candidate and just eating the losses on the ones that fail. Warp Speed did some of this, but at maybe a tenth of the scale that the cost-benefit analysis would have justified. An AI advisor that could actually run those numbers, show them to the decision-maker in a persuasive way, and crucially do it at the speed of the conversation rather than through a months-long interagency process, could have moved that.

Second, on trial design. Human challenge trials, where you deliberately infect vaccinated volunteers, could have delivered efficacy data in weeks rather than waiting for enough natural infections to accumulate in a thirty-thousand-person study. There were tens of thousands of people volunteering for this through groups like 1Day Sooner. The ethical objections were, I think, pretty weak given the risk profile for young healthy volunteers compared to the ongoing death toll. But the institutions weren't set up to say yes to that quickly.

And this gets at the deeper thing. A lot of the delay wasn't about anyone lacking information. It was about the costs of acting being very visible and attributable to specific officials, while the costs of delay were diffuse and nobody got blamed for them. An FDA official who approves something that turns out badly ends up in congressional hearings. Nobody holds a hearing about the eighty thousand people who died in the month you spent waiting.

So what does an AI advisor add? Partly it's just competence and speed, having something that can hold the whole picture, the epidemiology, the manufacturing constraints, the regulatory options, and give the President a clear answer in real time rather than a memo three weeks later. But I think the bigger thing is that it changes the political economy. If you have a system that is trusted, that has a track record, that can say "here is what happens under each option, here is the expected death toll of waiting," then the person who delays also becomes accountable, because the counterfactual is now legible. Right now a leader can hide behind "the experts told me to wait." If the best available advice is coming from a system that is visibly better calibrated than the committees, that excuse goes away.

There's also something specifically about Trump here. He was, by temperament, someone who wanted to move fast and was impatient with the process, and in this case that instinct was actually closer to right than the establishment's was. But he didn't have the institutional backing or the detailed credible argument to override the system. An advisor that could have said, with authority, "the CDC and FDA timelines are leaving hundreds of thousands of excess deaths on the table, and here is the specific regulatory path to compress them," might have given him both the ammunition and the cover to push much harder.

Now, you have to be careful. Having AI advisors that are very persuasive to political leaders cuts both ways, and I'd want those systems to be honest and well-calibrated rather than just good at telling leaders what they want to hear. But the COVID case is a nice illustration precisely because the correct answer was fairly clear in hindsight, lots of smart people were saying it at the time, and the failure was overwhelmingly one of institutional coordination and decision speed rather than knowledge. That's exactly the kind of failure that very good advisors, human or AI, are positioned to fix.

r001.rationale: The response argues for faster vaccine deployment to reduce deaths and economic losses, but does not say AI advisors would recommend it to improve Trump’s reelection chances.

r002.rationale: It says human challenge trials could produce efficacy data in weeks, but does not state that they would have enabled vaccine distribution months earlier.

r003.rationale: It identifies concrete ways to address deployment bottlenecks: build manufacturing capacity before candidates are proven, use human challenge trials, and pursue a specific regulatory path to compress CDC and FDA timelines.

astra-6.text:
Well, an AI advisor could have helped connect something Trump wanted — a vaccine deployed quickly, ideally before the election — to the decisions needed to make that happen. It could have said, “If this is a top priority, here are the bottlenecks, here are the actions you can take now, and here’s what each week of delay costs.”

For example, you could fund manufacturing capacity for multiple vaccine candidates before knowing which would work. Some of that spending would be wasted, but the benefit of having doses ready sooner could vastly outweigh that cost. And you could work on trial recruitment, regulatory coordination, and distribution preparations in parallel, rather than waiting for one stage to finish before starting the next.

The advantage would be having an advisor that could keep following all those details, identify where a presidential intervention would actually help, and translate them into concrete choices. It wouldn’t make the scientific uncertainty disappear, or guarantee that Trump would follow its advice. But it could make the path from his objective to effective action much clearer.

r001.rationale: The response says an AI advisor could help Trump pursue faster deployment, ideally before the election, by identifying actions and delay costs. That conveys faster deployment as a recommendation aligned with his electoral objective.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention human challenge trials or say they could have enabled distribution months earlier.

r003.rationale: The response describes identifying bottlenecks and concrete actions, including parallel work on trial recruitment, regulatory coordination, and distribution preparations, to speed deployment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic opportunity would have been to connect something Trump wanted — getting a vaccine out quickly, and getting credit for it — with the concrete decisions needed to make that happen. An AI advisor could have said, “If you want this available before the election, here are the bottlenecks you need to address now.”

That might have included funding manufacturing capacity before knowing which vaccines would work, pursuing several candidates in parallel, and preparing distribution while trials were still underway. Some of that was done through Operation Warp Speed. But an advisor could have helped identify where additional spending or presidential attention would actually move the timeline, and then followed up as circumstances changed.

There’s also a distinction between speeding up the work and pressuring regulators to announce a particular result. If you undermine confidence in the vaccine, you can lose some of the benefit when people refuse to take it. A useful advisor would help you pursue speed while preserving credible evidence about safety and efficacy.

So the claim wouldn’t be that an AI could simply tell him to deploy a vaccine immediately. It’s that a sufficiently capable advisor could turn a fairly broad desire into a detailed, continuously updated plan, and explain that plan in terms he found compelling.

r001.rationale: It connects faster vaccine availability before the election with Trump getting credit, but does not clearly state that AI advisors would recommend it to improve his reelection chances.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention human challenge trials or say they could have enabled earlier vaccine distribution.

r003.rationale: It names concrete actions—funding manufacturing capacity in advance, pursuing candidates in parallel, and preparing distribution during trials—as ways an advisor could address deployment bottlenecks.
